questions.q: Two spheres, each of mass 1000 kg, have their centres 2.0 m apart. What is the gravitational force between them? (\(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-2}\))
questions.solution: \(F = \frac{Gm_{1}m_{2}}{r^{2}} = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 1000 \times 1000}{2.0^{2}} = 1.7 \times 10^{-5}\ \text{N}\). Forgetting to square the distance is the usual slip.

questions.q: The graph shows how the gravitational force between two masses varies with the distance between their centres. The distance is doubled from r to 2r. What happens to the force?

figure.alt: Force against distance: a curve that falls steeply at first and then more gradually as the distance increases, following an inverse square law. Dashed lines mark the force at distance r and at distance 2r.

questions.solution: Gravitational force follows an inverse square law: it is proportional to one over the distance squared. Doubling the distance divides the force by two squared, so it falls to a quarter.

questions.q: A planet has a mass of \(6.0 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}\) and a radius of \(6.4 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}\). What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (\(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-2}\))
questions.solution: \(g = \frac{GM}{r^{2}} = \frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.0 \times 10^{24}}{(6.4 \times 10^{6})^{2}} = 9.8\ \text{N kg}^{-1}\). Forgetting to square the radius is the usual slip.

questions.q: A satellite is at a height above the Earth's surface equal to twice the Earth's radius. How does the gravitational field strength there compare with its value at the surface?
questions.solution: Field strength depends on distance from the centre of the Earth, not height above the surface. The satellite is three radii from the centre, and \(g\) is proportional to one over distance squared, so it is one ninth of the surface value.

questions.q: What is gravitational field strength at a point?

options.A: The force per unit mass on a small mass placed at the point.
options.B: The work done per unit mass in bringing a small mass to the point.
options.C: The force between two masses of one kilogram.
options.D: The mass per unit volume at the point.

questions.solution: Gravitational field strength is force per unit mass, \(g = \frac{F}{m}\), measured in newtons per kilogram. Work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity is the gravitational potential.

questions.q: What is the gravitational potential at a point?

options.A: The force per unit mass at the point.
options.B: The work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to the point.
options.C: The kinetic energy of a mass placed at the point.
options.D: The work done in moving a small mass from the point to the surface.

questions.solution: Gravitational potential is the work done per unit mass in moving a small mass from infinity to that point. It is measured in joules per kilogram and is zero at infinity.

questions.q: What is the gravitational potential at the surface of a planet of mass \(6.0 \times 10^{24}\ \text{kg}\) and radius \(6.4 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}\)? (\(G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-2}\))
questions.solution: \(V = -\frac{GM}{r} = -\frac{6.67 \times 10^{-11} \times 6.0 \times 10^{24}}{6.4 \times 10^{6}} = -6.3 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\). The radius is not squared for potential, and the value is negative.

questions.q: Why is gravitational potential always negative?

options.A: Because gravitational forces are very weak.
options.C: Because potential is measured from the surface of the planet.
options.D: Because it is zero at infinity and work must be done to move a mass away against the attractive force.

questions.solution: Potential is defined as zero at infinity. Gravity is always attractive, so work has to be done on a mass to move it out to infinity. A mass nearer the planet therefore has less potential energy than zero: its potential is negative.

questions.q: The gravitational potential at the surface of a planet is \(-6.3 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\). What is the escape velocity from its surface?
questions.solution: To escape, the kinetic energy per unit mass must equal the size of the potential: \(\frac{1}{2}v^{2} = 6.3 \times 10^{7}\). So \(v = \sqrt{2 \times 6.3 \times 10^{7}} = 1.1 \times 10^{4}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\). It does not depend on the mass of the object.

questions.q: A satellite is moved to a circular orbit with four times the radius. What happens to its orbital period?

options.B: It increases by a factor of four.
options.C: It increases by a factor of eight.
options.D: It increases by a factor of sixteen.

questions.solution: For circular orbits, the period squared is proportional to the radius cubed. Four cubed is sixty-four, so the period squared rises by a factor of sixty-four and the period by its square root, a factor of eight.

options.A: It orbits above the equator once every 24 hours, in the direction the Earth spins.
options.B: It orbits over the poles once every 24 hours.
options.C: It stays at rest in space while the Earth turns beneath it.
options.D: It orbits close to the Earth, several times a day.

questions.solution: A geostationary satellite orbits in the plane of the equator with a period of 24 hours, in the same direction as the Earth's rotation. It therefore stays above the same point on the ground, which suits communications. Low polar orbits are used for imaging.

questions.q: A satellite is in a circular orbit of radius \(7.0 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m}\) around the Earth. What is its speed? (For the Earth, \(GM = 4.0 \times 10^{14}\ \text{N m}^{2}\ \text{kg}^{-1}\))
questions.solution: Gravity provides the centripetal force: \(\frac{GMm}{r^{2}} = \frac{mv^{2}}{r}\). So \(v = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}} = \sqrt{\frac{4.0 \times 10^{14}}{7.0 \times 10^{6}}} = 7.6 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).

questions.q: A satellite moves from a low circular orbit to a higher circular orbit. What happens to its kinetic energy and its gravitational potential energy?

options.C: Kinetic energy increases and potential energy decreases.
options.D: Kinetic energy decreases and potential energy increases.

questions.solution: In a higher orbit the satellite moves more slowly, so its kinetic energy is smaller. It is further from the Earth, so its potential energy is greater (less negative). The gain in potential energy is twice the loss of kinetic energy, so its total energy rises.

questions.q: A mass is moved along a gravitational equipotential surface. How much work is done against gravity?

options.B: It depends on the distance moved.

questions.solution: Every point on an equipotential surface has the same potential. Work done is mass times change in potential, and the change is zero, so no work is done. Equipotentials are always at right angles to the field lines.

questions.q: A 500 kg satellite is raised through a change in gravitational potential of \(2.0 \times 10^{7}\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\). How much work is done on it?
questions.solution: Work done is mass times the change in potential: \(\Delta W = m\Delta V = 500 \times 2.0 \times 10^{7} = 1.0 \times 10^{10}\ \text{J}\).

questions.q: Which is a difference between gravitational fields and electric fields?

options.A: Gravitational forces are always attractive; electric forces can attract or repel.
options.B: Gravitational forces follow an inverse square law; electric forces do not.
options.C: Gravitational fields act at a distance; electric fields need contact.
options.D: Gravitational fields can be shown by field lines; electric fields cannot.

questions.solution: Mass is always positive, so gravity only attracts. Charge can be positive or negative, so electric forces can attract or repel. Both fields act at a distance, can be drawn with field lines, and follow inverse square laws for point masses and point charges.
